transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Let's look at your research design. Aisha, remind me of your research question.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: We want to find out whether students who spend more time on social media experience higher stress during exams.

transcript.speaker: S3
transcript.text: An online questionnaire sent to second-year students, using the university mailing list. We expect around three hundred responses.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Three hundred would be good, but I'm concerned about self-selection. Students who are very stressed may be less likely to complete a questionnaire, and those who are heavy social media users may be more likely to respond to a message sent online. Either could distort your results.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: We hadn't considered that. Could we offer an incentive, like a prize draw?

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: That can help, but it introduces its own bias. You might also approach students in person, in the library, for example, though that has a different bias because it only reaches those who study there. The honest approach is to acknowledge the limitation in your discussion section.

transcript.speaker: S3
transcript.text: What about the analysis? We're planning to calculate a correlation.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Good, but remember what a correlation can and cannot show. Suppose you find that heavy users are more stressed. That doesn't mean social media causes stress. Perhaps stressed students turn to their phones for relief. Or a third factor, such as poor sleep, could affect both.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: So we should use cautious language, like is associated with.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Precisely. Now, your questions. How will you measure stress?

transcript.speaker: S3
transcript.text: We found a standard scale with ten questions, widely used in psychology.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Excellent. Using an established scale is far better than inventing your own, since its reliability has already been tested. But how will you measure social media use?

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: By asking people to estimate their daily hours.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: That's the weak point. People are notoriously poor at estimating screen time. Many phones record usage automatically. Could participants share that data?

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: It might, which is why your ethics application needs to explain exactly what you will collect, how it will be stored and when it will be deleted. A simple solution is to ask them to report the figure from their phone settings, without sharing the full record.

transcript.speaker: S2
transcript.text: That's a good compromise. Should we run a pilot?

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Absolutely. Test the questionnaire with ten or fifteen students first. You'd be surprised how often a question that seems clear to the author confuses everyone else. Do it before the end of this month, so that you can still make changes.
